analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. John Thune with 35 Republican cosponsors and none from the other party, the estate-tax repeal bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, the two taxes that fall on very large inheritances, effective the day it was signed. It would keep a gift tax but cut its top rate from 40% to 35% and set a $10 million lifetime gift exemption, while taxing certain transfers into trust so the wealthiest families could not simply give everything away before dying.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — those above the exemption threshold (roughly $11 million per person under the law in effect in 2019) — would keep the 40% tax they currently owe on everything above that line, often millions of dollars per estate. Very wealthy individuals planning large lifetime gifts would also benefit from the lower 35% gift-tax rate and the $10 million exemption.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the estate tax entirely for people dying after enactment, so heirs of the largest estates would no longer owe the 40% tax on inheritances above the exemption.
Eliminates the generation-skipping transfer tax, which otherwise taxes large bequests that skip a generation, such as money left directly from a grandparent to grandchildren.
Cuts the top gift-tax rate from 40% to 35% and sets a $10 million lifetime gift exemption with an inflation adjustment, making it cheaper to move wealth during life.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so the lost estate-tax collections would have to be made up by other taxpayers, cuts to federal programs, or additional borrowing.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and generation-skipping taxes would permanently remove the federal tax that falls almost entirely on the largest inheritances, and the bill provides no replacement revenue — the cost would surface as deficits, other taxes, or cuts elsewhere.
The repeal takes effect the moment the bill is signed, so the estates of people dying after that date would owe nothing, an immediate windfall for the largest estates then in settlement.
Cutting the top gift-tax rate to 35% with a $10 million lifetime exemption would let the wealthiest families shift large amounts to heirs during life at a lower rate than current law imposes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are extraordinarily concentrated: the estate tax only applies above a large exemption, so the winners would be a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year, while the revenue loss spreads across every federal taxpayer and every program that depends on federal funding. The bill offered nothing for ordinary households and included no way to pay for the cut. The bill's own design acknowledges the stakes — it keeps a gift tax with anti-trust-avoidance rules only because outright repeal of all transfer taxes would let the richest families give everything away untaxed before death.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on January 24, 2019 with 29 original cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The cosponsor list grew to 35, all Republicans, including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Finance Committee Chair Chuck Grassley.
The Finance Committee never held a markup and the Senate never took it up; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax remained on the books, so the very wealthy families that would have saved millions gained nothing. The public was spared the revenue loss and the shifted tax burden that repeal would have brought.

for.name: John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 35 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 35 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

for.name: Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Repeatedly called for repealing the estate tax, which he labeled the 'death tax', throughout his term, though he took no recorded action on this specific bill.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never scheduled a committee markup or vote; it died in his committee.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor in two years.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no formal party split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Very wealthy families and their heirs
industries.note: The estate tax only applies above a large exemption (about $11 million per person under 2019 law), so repeal is a direct windfall of millions per estate for the few thousand largest inheritances each year. The revenue those estates currently contribute would be lost to everyone else.

A large share of estate planning exists to reduce estate-tax exposure, so full repeal would shrink that business. The bill keeps a gift tax at a 35% top rate and taxes certain transfers into trust, leaving some planning work to do.
